title: Not yet
hookLine: many Sikhs are not yet amritdhari and are still fully welcome
tomorrow: Chacha Ji asks at dinner: so, when's your amrit? what does she say?

cards: Group photos have a way of making you count who's in the picture and who isn't. Simran scrolls through Jasleen's: the new kirpan, the whole family beaming. Simran has decided, for now, not yet.
She's at peace with it until late at night, when she texts Maya, her best friend: does that make me less of a Sikh? Maya doesn't answer with an opinion.
She answers with a line her grandma always quotes, from a story in the Bible.

teach.h: THE SAME FLOOR, THE SAME LANGAR.
teach.b: One question today: where does someone stand before they've taken the step? The Sikh answer is in the room itself.
At the gurdwara, everyone sits on the same floor, hears the same Granth, takes the same karah prashad and eats the same langar. Nobody checks at the door who is amritdhari.
Guru Arjan, on ang 1299, says it in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. A Sikh who hasn't taken amrit is part of the sangat, learning and welcome.

teach.h: LUKE 15:20: YET A GREAT WAY OFF.
teach.b: In the Gospel of Luke, a son who left home is walking back, and the text says: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him."
Yet a great way off. The welcome runs out to meet him before he arrives.
That's the shared thing: in both, the welcome doesn't wait for the finish line. And the honest difference. The son in Luke's story is coming back after wasting everything, ready to say he's sorry.
Simran's not yet isn't a wrong turn. She hasn't wandered off; she's still walking toward a step Sikhs take when they're ready. Two different roads, and on both, someone is already at the door.

how: At the gurdwara everyone sits together, hears the Guru Granth Sahib, and shares karah prashad and langar, whether or not they have taken amrit.

o: being kept out of the gurdwara for a while
not having taken amrit for now, still fully welcome
having left the Sikh path after taking amrit

games.q: the welcome, in two traditions — tap the pairs.

s: only amritdhari Sikhs may eat langar or sit in the sangat
everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same langar; nobody checks at the door.
in Luke's story, the father runs while the son is still far off
"when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him… and ran."
Simran's not yet is just like the son in Luke's story
the honest difference: the son returns after wasting everything; Simran hasn't wandered off at all.

games.q: a new member joins your choir but can't read music yet. someone says she should sit at the back until she can. going by today?
o: welcome her into the choir now; the welcome doesn't wait for the finish line.
let her watch from the back until she's caught up.
tell her she'll belong once she's proven she can keep up.
games.why: in the sangat nobody checks at the door, and in Luke's story the father runs out before the son arrives.

practice: Bring to mind someone who's partway along a road: learning a language, new on your team, finding their way back to something. Send them a short message that welcomes them exactly where they are, with no 'yet' in it.
Then set the phone face down and sit.

wordCard.voice: Not yet. Not having taken amrit, for now, while still fully part of the sangat.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sangat, the gathered community, all on the same floor.

carryVoice: Your line: not yet is fine. The welcome doesn't wait for the finish line. Good night.

sources.ref: Ang 1299 (Kanra, Guru Arjan: na ko bairee nahee bigaanaa sagal sang ham kau ban aaee), paraphrased

sources.q: But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
